articleTitle: IEE Colloquium on 'Light Rapid Transit On-Street' (Digest No.80)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Light Rapid Transit On-Street
IEE Colloquium on Light Rapid Transit On-Street
abstract: The South Yorkshire Passenger Transport Executive (SYPTE) intend to build a network of light rail transit (Supertram) routes in order to improve public transport in the South Yorkshire region. Supertram will provide a fast, modern, reliable, high quality public transport system, with excellent access for the mobility impaired. Parts of the system will run on the streets along with some or all ordinary vehicles. The article discusses signalling to ensure priority, and the relationship between journey time and likely levels of patronage.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A British traffic signal control and detection system for LRV priority at signalled intersections
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Light Rapid Transit On-Street
abstract: This paper describes the techniques and equipment used to provide priority to rail vehicles at signalled intersections in light rapid transit (LRT) systems sharing track with road users. The system is operational in the New Territories, Hong Kong as part of the Tuen Mun-Yuen Long LRT for the Kowloon Canton Railway Corporation. There are seven routes operated over 23 km of double track including 41 stops and 50 signalled intersections. A fleet of 70 vehicles is regularly in service. Each rail vehicle is equipped with an individually coded transponder which communicates with a trackside outstation via detector loops laid between the rails. As the vehicle passes over the detector, the transponder identifies its route and its run number. This information is processed locally by the outstation and used to request traffic phases and points switching and to provide supervisory status information to the operations control centre. The management of intersections is accomplished locally.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: FLEXSYT: a case study on LRT with Plessey's T200 principles
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Light Rapid Transit On-Street
abstract: As part of the implementation programme of the traffic control system for the Tuen Mun-Yuen Long light rapid transit (LRT) system in Hong Kong, in which light rail traffic runs on streets along with other traffic, it was proposed that a computerised simulation method of control should be included. The program FLEXSYT was found to fit the needs of the proposed simulation best and the Dutch Ministry of Transport was asked to do a case study on whether there is a need to use main road detection at the MN5 junction and what are the consequences of giving priority to LRT-vehicles at that junction. Plessey's T200 signal controller is used.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Light Rapid Transit On-Street
abstract: Discusses the underlying reasons for current UK interest in light rapid transit (LRT). LRT represents a technology which is highly relevant to key current urban problems. It can and should provide a means of improving public transport to revive old urban areas and sustain the growth and vitality of booming city centres. However, implementation of an LRT project is fraught with difficulty, and requires a consistent and long-sighted sense of purpose that is difficult to achieve. Thus it is possible that many schemes will not come to fruition, irrespective of the underlying soundness of their rationale. Street running is an essential component of many of the current schemes and will prove equally vital in securing finance. Imaginative ideas and delicate judgement will be necessary to secure the best possible deal for the LRT passenger and other highway users.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Electromagnetic compatibility in light rail system
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Light Rapid Transit On-Street
abstract: With the increasingly sophisticated electronics on vehicles and elsewhere there is plenty of scope for the construction of light rapid transit (LRT) systems that are adversely affected by their environment and that affect other systems. Electromagnetic compatibility is not something that can be added at the end of the job; it has to be designed in from the start. The key to successful EMC is to recognise the need for an EMC strategy when the project is conceived and to ensure that it is handled as one of the engineering interfaces. As with most interfaces there is no substitute for an experienced systems engineer who treats the LRT as a total system. Merely adopting a specification from another field, however good, is unlikely to be successful.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: LRT on-street running-design and safety issues
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Light Rapid Transit On-Street
abstract: With the upsurge of interest in light rail transit (LRT) and the desire to keep construction costs down, serious consideration is being given in many cities to mixed running of LRT and other traffic on the streets. This brings many planning, design and safety problems, and the paper highlights some of them and indicates an approach to solving them, based upon experience gained in British cities and more particularly on the Tuen Mun to Yuen Long system in Hong Kong. This system represented a far more difficult challenge than most, with high LRT vehicle flows (some junctions have to cope with 100 an hour), high traffic flows, and very high levels of pedestrian activity. In addition, general observance of signals and road regulations is not of the highest order, and even the slow moving tram system on Hong Kong Island suffers an average of 2 injury accidents a week. Despite this, and a degree of undeserved adverse publicity, the system and its integration with road traffic and pedestrians is very successful and it provides a very good public transport service.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Light Rapid Transit On-Street
abstract: The introduction of light rapid transit (LRT) systems with rail vehicles on streets is discussed, the British situation being compared with that in Europe where trams were developed, not withdrawn. The articulated vehicles, akin to trains, proposed for use in Manchester are described. Signals are discussed, and it is suggested that a set of signals additional to normal traffic lights is required-horizontal and vertical rows of dots are suggested. The signalling in Manchester is to be centrally controlled by computer. LRT vehicles will be detected, and vehicles on different routes will be distinguished; the signals will then be set according to a scheme of priority.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
